newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FROTH OFF EUROPE BEER MARKET - DUTCH RABOBANK.
newsitem.headline: FROTH OFF EUROPE BEER MARKET - DUTCH RABOBANK.

text.p: Beer consumption in western Europe is set to decline by 0.3 percent a year until the end of the century, Dutch financial group Rabobank said in a report on the world's beer markets released on Friday.
Total European beer market will show annual growth of 0.4 percent until 2000. Beer consumption in central Europe and the former Soviet Union will increase by an annual 2.5 percent.

World beer consumption -- set to grow 1.7 percent anually until 2000, when the world will drink some 1,320 million hectolitres -- was divided into several regions showing more or less similar growth patterns.

South East Asia and China were set to show the biggest rise in consumption, adding an annual 6.4 percent until the end of the century. Asian beer consumption as a whole was set to increase by 4.5 percent a year.

"Beer consumption tends to increase with rises in income in the lower-income developing countries in particular," the report said, indicating the beer industry should turn towards countries with expanding economies and strong population growth.
Growth in beer market volume had outstripped per capita consumption growth in the Asian region, showing population growth was primarily driving the increase in beer consumption.
Rabo said beer consumption in South America would increase by an annual 2.8 percent until the year 2000.
But it said Europe and the United States were saturated markets, showing stagnating or declining trends in consumption.

The report noted that margins would come under increasing pressure as supermarkets wielded a greater power over prices. Europe also suffered from a production overcapacity of around 10 percent, mainly in Germany, UK and Spain.
